prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna is in the middle of a terrible crisis, and he tells Krishna that his mind feels like the wind. He says it is restless, turbulent, and stubborn, and that trying to hold it is like trying to catch the air. Krishna does not argue. He agrees, and then he offers a way forward. The mind is hard to hold, but it can be trained through practice and letting go.
verse.for_you: You are on your phone for seven hours, and your mind will not settle. This is not a failure in you. It is simply what a mind does when it has never been taught to rest. You do not need to force it.

verse.line: Raise your mind like a child: gently, patiently, little by little, never by force.
verse.translation: With evenness and gentle coaxing, not in a rush but little by little, by steady effort, look after the child that is your mind.
verse.why: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

prasang.title: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha is speaking to Rama, who is young and full of sorrow over his past. Vasishtha tells him to look after his own mind like a child. He says to do this with evenness and gentle coaxing, not in a rush, but little by little, with steady effort. He tells Rama not to grieve over what was never in his hands, because today's effort shapes tomorrow.
verse.for_you: You are building your life right now. Your past effort shaped today, and today's effort will shape tomorrow. You do not need to force your mind to be still. You only need to steer it gently, like raising a child. Little by little, with steady effort, you can teach it to rest.

prasang.title: Yajnavalkya on desire and death
prasang.summary: Yajnavalkya explains what happens at death with images of a caterpillar and a goldsmith. A person becomes what they desire, will and do; one who knows the self has nothing left to fret about. Know it while you are here, he says, don't brood over many words, and live calm and collected.
prasang.lesson: You become what you desire and do; know what matters while you are here.

verse.meaning: Yajnavalkya is talking to King Janaka about what happens when a person truly knows themselves. He tells him not to brood over many words, because that only tires the voice. He says to know the one thing, and let wisdom grow from it. If you know what truly matters, you will become it. You do not need to carry a hundred thoughts at once.
verse.for_you: You do not need to hold every thought at once. Pick one thing to focus on today, maybe a single page of your notes, and let your mind rest there. You become what you do, not what you scroll through.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna to fix his mind on him alone and let his understanding settle. From there, he will dwell in him. It is a simple instruction to rest the mind on one thing and let everything else fall away. The mind settles when it has one place to land.
verse.for_you: Give your mind one place to land today. It could be the feeling of your feet on the floor or the words on one line of your book. Let your thinking settle there, and let the rest wait.

story.title: Karunya stops acting: knowledge and action as two wings
story.story_hook: Karunya came home from his studies so full of questions that he stopped doing anything at all.
story.summary: A student asks the sage Agastya whether freedom comes from action or from knowledge. Agastya answers with a story: young Karunya, confused by two scriptures, simply stopped doing anything, and his father had to show him that understanding and action work together.
story.lesson: Don't freeze while you wait to be sure. Understanding and action have to fly together.

script: You are trying to study, but your mind keeps running. You pick up your phone, and it runs there. It does not stop. You feel the stress of it, but you cannot name the cause.

Arjuna is on a battlefield. He is in a terrible crisis, and he turns to Krishna. He tells him that his mind is restless, turbulent, and stubborn. He says trying to hold it is like trying to catch the wind. Krishna does not argue. He agrees, and then he offers a way forward. And Arjuna says:
चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम्, तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम्.
In plain words: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.

The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind. This is easier said than done, because you were never taught to let it rest. You just learned to fill every gap with noise.
You do not need to force it. Give it one thing. Let your eyes rest on a single word, and let your mind follow. That is enough for now.
The mind is hard to hold, but it can be trained.

depth.life: You are sitting with your books open but your eyes are on the screen. The hours pass and you feel the anxiety rising, yet you do not know why you cannot put it down or where to begin.
depth.points: The mind is not an enemy to be conquered. It is a habit that has not been taught stillness. It moves because it has never been shown how to rest.
depth.practice: Put the phone face down and sit with your eyes closed for three minutes without trying to stop any thoughts.
depth.question: What would it feel like to let your mind move for just a little while?
